(CNN) -- Rioting has flared near Belfast on Saturday after the arrests of three men in the killings of two soldiers in Northern Ireland last week, police said. Two people in masks prepare to throw petrol bombs Saturday in Lurgan, Northern Ireland. Petrol bombs have been hurled at police in Lurgan, a town in County Armagh, 20 miles west of Belfast, police in Northern Ireland said. There are gangs of youths on the streets, authorities said, but there have been no arrests or injuries. Police announced the arrests on Saturday and said the three men have been taken to the police service's Serious Crime Suite in County Antrim. One of them, a dissident republican named Colin Duffy, is from Lurgan. They are the first arrests in connection with the March 7 shootings, which were the first fatal attack on British troops in the province for more than 12 years. The two British soldiers were shot dead at a base in Massereene, in Antrim, as they were preparing to ship out for duty in Afghanistan. The soldiers, Cengiz "Pat" Azimkar, 21, and Mark Quinsey, 23, had already packed their bags and changed into desert uniforms, authorities said. Two masked gunmen with automatic rifles shot them as the soldiers picked up a pizza delivery at the barracks, authorities said. Two other soldiers and the two pizza delivery men were seriously wounded. The shooting has sparked fears of a return to the sectarian violence that Northern Ireland suffered until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, a period known as The Troubles. A militant splinter group, the Real IRA, reportedly claimed it had carried out the attack on the soldiers. Two days after the soldiers were killed, a police officer was killed in a shooting southwest of Belfast. Constable Stephen Carroll was one of four officers who were responding to call in Craigavon when his vehicle came under fire and he was killed. Three people have been arrested in connection with the police officer's death. The Continuity IRA, a republican splinter group that does not accept the Good Friday Agreement, said it had killed Carroll, Britain's Press Association reported. Politicians from across the political spectrum have condemned the killings, with Sinn Fein deputy leader Martin McGuinness calling the killers "traitors to the island of Ireland." Sinn Fein is a predominantly Catholic party that wants Northern Ireland to leave the United Kingdom and become part of the Republic of Ireland. The party is widely thought to be linked to the Irish Republican Army. Danny Kennedy, deputy leader of the loyalist Ulster Unionist Party, which wants Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom, also condemned the attack as "wicked and murderous."

The unrest centered on Lurgan, County Armagh, where rioters hurled petrol bombs at police officers during the disturbances. The killings, and the subsequent unrest, have stirred deep anxieties that Northern Ireland could be sliding back toward the sectarian violence known as The Troubles—a decades-long conflict between republican and unionist factions that resulted in thousands of deaths before it was largely brought to an end by the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. The group gained international notoriety following the 1998 Omagh bombing, which killed 29 people and remains one of the deadliest atrocities of the Troubles era, despite occurring after the Good Friday Agreement was signed.

# Northern Ireland Unrest of 2009: A Return to Violence

## The Massereene Barracks Attack

On the evening of March 7, 2009, Northern Ireland experienced its first fatal paramilitary attack on security forces in over a decade. Gunmen opened fire on soldiers outside Massereene Barracks in Antrim, killing two young British Army soldiers, Sappers Mark Quinsey, 23, from Birmingham, and Patrick Azimkar, 21, from London.

The soldiers, both members of the Royal Engineers, were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan and were collecting a pizza delivery at the barracks gate when attackers opened fire with automatic weapons. Two other soldiers and two civilian delivery workers were wounded in the assault. The attackers reportedly continued firing at the victims as they lay wounded on the ground, a detail that intensified public revulsion at the killings.

The Real IRA, a dissident republican paramilitary group opposed to the peace process, claimed responsibility for the attack. The organization had rejected the 1998 Good Friday Agreement and the broader peace settlement that had largely ended three decades of sectarian violence known as "the Troubles."

## Political Reaction and Condemnation

The killings drew swift and near-universal condemnation across Northern Ireland's political spectrum. Notably, Martin McGuinness, then deputy first minister and former IRA commander, condemned the attackers as "traitors to the island of Ireland," signaling how thoroughly mainstream republicanism had moved away from armed struggle. Sinn Féin's stance was significant, demonstrating a unified political front against a return to violence.

First Minister Peter Robinson and other unionist leaders joined in condemning the attack, while British Prime Minister Gordon Brown and other officials expressed concern that the killings could destabilize the fragile peace process, though most analysts believed the political institutions established under the Good Friday Agreement were resilient enough to withstand the attack.

## Further Violence: The Death of Constable Stephen Carroll

Two days after the barracks shooting, on March 9, 2009, dissident republicans struck again. Constable Stephen Carroll, a 48-year-old Catholic officer with the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), was shot dead while responding to a call in Craigavon, County Armagh. The Continuity IRA, another dissident republican group, claimed responsibility for his killing.

Carroll's murder was particularly significant as the first police officer killed in Northern Ireland since the PSNI replaced the Royal Ulster Constabulary in 2001 as part of policing reforms under the peace agreement.

## Arrests and Investigations

In the aftermath of the attacks, police launched intensive investigations. Several individuals were arrested in connection with the Massereene Barracks shooting and Carroll's murder. Among those detained were individuals linked to dissident republican networks in County Armagh and elsewhere.

Colin Duffy, a well-known republican figure who had previously faced (and been acquitted of) charges related to earlier killings during the Troubles, was arrested in connection with Carroll's murder. Various other suspects were held for questioning under anti-terrorism legislation, though not all arrests led to charges, reflecting the difficulties security forces faced in gathering evidence against clandestine dissident cells.

## Sporadic Rioting and Continued Unrest

The killings occurred against a backdrop of episodic street violence that had periodically flared in interface areas of Belfast and other towns, particularly during the traditional marching season and around contentious commemorative dates. While the March 2009 killings were primarily attributed to dissident paramilitary action rather than street rioting per se, they heightened tensions in some republican and loyalist communities.

Sporadic clashes with police, particularly in areas with a history of dissident republican sympathy such as parts of Lurgan and Craigavon, saw isolated incidents of disorder in the following weeks, as security forces increased patrols and searches in these areas, sometimes prompting local backlash from residents wary of heavy-handed policing reminiscent of earlier decades.

## Aftermath and Legacy

The 2009 attacks marked a sobering reminder that despite more than a decade of relative peace, small but violent dissident republican factions remained committed to armed conflict. The killings prompted increased security cooperation between British and Irish authorities and renewed efforts to counter dissident recruitment and activity.

Public marches and vigils were held in Antrim and elsewhere to honor the victims, with cross-community support demonstrating that the vast majority of people in Northern Ireland, from both traditions, rejected a return to violence.

Ultimately, while deeply shocking, the attacks did not succeed in derailing the peace process or triggering the widespread sectarian violence dissidents may have hoped to provoke. The Northern Ireland Assembly continued to function, and the years following 2009 saw continued, if uneven, progress in the broader peace process, even as dissident republican violence persisted at a lower level in subsequent years.
